why.correct: Each location peaks in turn: rough ER at 0 min, Golgi at about 20 min, vesicles at about 60 min, and the outside keeps rising to the end. Label moves from one place to the next, so the order of the peaks is the order of the path.
options: The peaks come in this order (0, 20, 60 and 120+ minutes), which is the path of a secreted protein.
At time 0 the rough ER already holds 90% of the label and the Golgi only 4%, so the protein cannot start in the Golgi.
Vesicles peak at about 60 minutes, well after the Golgi peaks at about 20 minutes, so the vesicles come after the Golgi.
Almost no label is outside the cell until 40 minutes, after the Golgi has peaked, so the protein leaves last, not second.

why.correct: At 40 minutes the Golgi holds 30% and the secretory vesicles 45%: 30 + 45 = 75%.
Proteins still travel from the rough ER to the Golgi, but they cannot leave it in vesicles, so label piles up in the Golgi and few labeled proteins reach the vesicles or the outside.
options: The drug acts on vesicles leaving the Golgi, not on those leaving the ER, so proteins still move on from the ER and reach the Golgi.
Label enters the Golgi as usual but cannot leave it, so it collects there instead of moving on.
Secreted proteins leave a cell inside vesicles that fuse with the membrane; with no vesicles from the Golgi, they cannot get out.
Secretory vesicles form from the Golgi, so blocking budding leaves fewer of them, not more.

why.correct: If proteins were made in the Golgi, label would appear there first and only later in the ER. The data show the reverse: the ER is labeled first, and its loss matches the Golgi's gain.
options: This shows the protein leaves the cell, but says nothing about whether it passed through the ER or the Golgi first.
The ER is labeled first and loses label as the Golgi gains it, the opposite of what the claim predicts.
This concerns the later steps; it does not show where the protein started.
A small leftover share in the ER fits either order, so it cannot refute the claim.

why.correct: A protein bound for export is built by a ribosome attached to the rough ER. The growing chain goes straight into the ER, so the label is inside the ER almost as soon as it is built into protein.
options: Every protein is built by ribosomes; the ER does not link amino acids into proteins by itself.
Ribosomes work in the cytoplasm and on the rough ER, not inside the nucleus; the nucleolus only assembles their pieces.
This is how proteins for export are made: built on the rough ER and threaded into it as they grow.
Proteins made on free ribosomes mostly stay in the cytosol; if this protein were made there, label would first collect in the cytosol.

why.correct: Enzymes are proteins, and proteins for export are made on the rough ER. Cell W has by far the most rough ER (20% of its volume).
options: Cell W's large rough ER fits a cell that builds and exports a lot of protein.
Cell X has little rough ER but much smooth ER, which makes lipids and breaks down toxins, not exported proteins.
Cell Y is mostly mitochondria, which fits a cell that uses a lot of ATP, not one that exports protein.
Cell Z's many lysosomes fit a cell that breaks material down inside itself, not one that exports enzymes.

why.correct: Smooth ER holds enzymes that detoxify drugs and poisons. Liver cells that must handle a steady supply of a drug build more smooth ER.
options: Breaking down drugs and toxins is a job of the smooth ER, so more drug leads to more smooth ER.
Lysosomes digest worn-out parts and engulfed material; they are not where liver cells detoxify drugs.
Rough ER builds proteins for export and membranes; the drug-handling enzymes work in the smooth ER.
Detoxifying a drug does not supply the cell's energy, and the cell still needs ATP from its mitochondria.

why.correct: Divide the two shares: 36% ÷ 6% = 6.0. Mitochondria take up six times as large a share of cell Y as of cell Z.
Mitochondria are where cellular respiration makes most of a cell's ATP. A cell that is 36% mitochondria, like a heart muscle cell, uses energy steadily and fast.
options: Exported proteins are built on the rough ER, and cell Y has almost none (1%).
This links the evidence (36% mitochondria) to the job of mitochondria (making ATP) correctly.
Lipids are made in the smooth ER, and cell Y has very little smooth ER (1%).
Digesting worn-out parts and engulfed material is the job of lysosomes, and cell Y has the fewest of the four.

why.correct: Many lysosomes fit the claim but do not show that bacteria are digested. Seeing bacteria inside vesicles merged with lysosomes is direct evidence of engulfing followed by digestion.
options: Free ribosomes make proteins for the cytosol; their number says nothing about engulfing bacteria.
Cell size alone does not show what a cell takes in or breaks down.
This directly shows bacteria taken in and delivered to the lysosomes' digestive enzymes.
Fewer mitochondria says the cell uses less ATP, not that it digests bacteria.

why.correct: The enzyme breaks down 42 to 46 µg per hour at pH 4.5 to 5.0, less on either side, and just 3 µg per hour at pH 7.2.
options: At pH 7.2 the enzyme breaks down only 3 µg per hour, the lowest value in the table.
This matches the table: a peak near pH 5, falling steeply toward neutral.
The values rise from 3.5 to 5.0 and then fall, so there is no steady rise.
The values range from 3 to 46 µg per hour, more than a fifteenfold difference.

why.correct: Its fastest pace is 46 µg per hour (pH 5.0); at pH 7.2 it is 3 µg per hour. 3 ÷ 46 × 100 = 6.5%, which rounds to 7%.
At the cytosol's pH (7.2) the enzyme breaks down only 3 µg per hour, against 46 at its best. A few leaked molecules work too slowly to do much damage.
options: This uses the table's value at pH 7.2 to explain the low damage.
The cytosol (pH 7.2) is less acidic than the lysosome (pH 4.5 to 5), and the enzyme works best in acid, not worst.
Cell proteins are built from the same 20 kinds of amino acids, so this does not explain the protection.
The table shows the enzyme works much more slowly, not faster, at the cytosol's pH.

why.correct: At a pH near 7 the enzymes work at a small fraction of their usual pace, so material delivered to lysosomes is broken down far more slowly and accumulates.
options: Raising the pH slows the enzymes, so breakdown is slower, not faster.
The drug changes the pH inside the lysosome; it does not release the enzymes, and at pH 7 they work slowly anyway.
Material keeps arriving but is digested far more slowly, so it builds up.
Nothing in the data says the cell stops making the enzyme; the problem is that the enzyme works poorly at the new pH.

why.correct: Every cell has a cell membrane, cytoplasm, DNA and ribosomes. A nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles, such as mitochondria and the Golgi, are found only in eukaryotes.
options: All cells build proteins on ribosomes, so prokaryotes and eukaryotes both have them.
Every cell is bounded by a cell membrane.
A prokaryote's DNA sits in the cytoplasm with no membrane around it; only eukaryotes have a nucleus.
Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles, found in eukaryotes but not prokaryotes.
All cells are filled with cytoplasm, the region inside the membrane.
The Golgi is part of the endomembrane system, which prokaryotes lack.

why.correct: Mitochondria (and chloroplasts) contain their own DNA and ribosomes, and they make some of the proteins they need.
options: Mitochondria carry their own ribosomes; these are not stray cytosol ribosomes, and ribosomes build proteins rather than take in fuel.
This is the known feature of mitochondria: their own DNA and ribosomes making some of their proteins.
Ribosomes build proteins; breaking proteins down is a lysosome's job.
Mitochondria do not contain rough ER; the ER is a separate organelle in the cytoplasm.

why.correct: Much of a cell's ATP is made by proteins set in the inner membrane. More folds pack more of that membrane, and so more of those proteins, into the same space.
options: The ATP-making proteins sit in the inner membrane, so less membrane means less ATP-making machinery, not more.
Outer size is the same, but the amount of inner membrane differs, and that membrane holds the ATP-making proteins.
This links the folds to their function: more inner membrane, more ATP-making proteins.
Mitochondrial DNA sits in the matrix; cristae are about membrane for making ATP, not DNA storage.

why.correct: The central vacuole stores water. When it shrinks, it presses less on the cytoplasm and cell wall, the cells go limp and the leaf droops. Organelle numbers do not change in a week.

variables.name: Volume of the central vacuole
variables.why: The central vacuole is mostly water; with too little water coming in from the roots, the cell loses water and the vacuole shrinks.

variables.name: Outward push of the cell contents against the cell wall
variables.why: A full central vacuole presses the cytoplasm against the wall and keeps the cell firm; a shrunken vacuole presses less, so the cell goes limp and the leaf droops.

variables.name: Number of chloroplasts in the cell
variables.why: A week of dry soil changes the cell's water content, not the number of chloroplasts it holds; the chloroplasts are still there.

why.correct: Instructions leave the nucleus as mRNA, ribosomes on the rough ER build the protein into the ER, vesicles carry it to the Golgi, the Golgi modifies and packages it, and a vesicle releases it at the cell membrane.
Microtubules are tracks along which motor proteins carry vesicles. Without the tracks, vesicles move slowly and randomly, so fewer reach the membrane and release their contents.
options: Ribosomes build proteins without microtubules, so protein is still made.
Vesicles travel along microtubules, so losing them slows delivery to the membrane.
Nothing about microtubules makes the Golgi fuse with the nucleus.
The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer that holds together without microtubules.

why.correct: The nucleolus, a dense region inside the nucleus, makes ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and joins it with proteins into ribosome pieces, which leave through nuclear pores.
options: This is the nucleolus's job: rRNA and ribosome assembly.
Cells do not store ATP in the nucleus; ATP is made and used continuously, mostly with the help of mitochondria.
Packaging proteins into vesicles is the Golgi complex's job.
Breaking down worn-out organelles is a lysosome's job.

why.correct: Lysosomes break down molecules with specific enzymes. Missing one enzyme means its target is delivered to the lysosomes but never digested, so it accumulates there.
options: Mitochondria do not take over a lysosome's digestive work, so the lipid is not cleared.
The disorder affects breakdown, not lipid making, so the lipid does not disappear.
The undigested lipid collects where it was supposed to be broken down.
Material sent to lysosomes for breakdown is not rerouted out of the cell through the Golgi.

why.correct: Surface area = 6 × 3² = 54 cm²; volume = 3³ = 27 cm³. 54 ÷ 27 = 2.0 per cm.
Volume reached = 8 − 1.73 = 6.27 cm³. 6.27 ÷ 8 × 100 = 78.4%, which rounds to 78%. (For the 1 cm cube it is over 99%; for the 3 cm cube about 61%.)
The depth is about 0.4 cm in every cube (the SDs overlap), but 0.4 cm covers nearly all of a 1 cm cube and much less of a 3 cm cube, whose center is 1.5 cm from any face.
options: The depths are all about 0.4 cm, so acid did not move faster into the larger cubes.
This is what the table shows: equal depth, so the reached share falls as the cube grows.
The depth is the same in all three cubes; what changes is the share of the volume that depth covers.
The 2 and 3 cm cubes still have pink volume left (1.73 and 10.6 cm³), so the acid did not reach all of them.

why.correct: The students chose the cube sizes (independent variable) and measured how far the acid got in and what share of each cube it reached (dependent variables).
options: Soaking time was held at 10 minutes for every cube, so it is a controlled variable, and cube size was chosen, not measured.
All cubes sat in the same vinegar, so its concentration was held constant, not varied.
Size was set by the students, and the acid's spread was measured in response.
The color change is how the acid's spread was seen; surface area ÷ volume follows from the size the students chose.

why.correct: Acid reaches about 0.4 cm from each face in 10 minutes. The slab is only 0.5 cm thick, so acid entering from the top and bottom meets in the middle. Its surface area ÷ volume is 40 cm² ÷ 8 cm³ = 5 per cm, higher than the cube's 3.
options: Equal volume does not mean equal exposure: the slab has more surface (40 cm² against 24 cm²) for the same volume.
Being thin puts every point close to a face, so the 0.4 cm the acid travels reaches the whole slab.
The slab's surface area ÷ volume is 5 per cm, higher than the cube's 3 per cm, not lower.
Acid enters through every face, and the large top and bottom faces are the slab's biggest surfaces.

why.correct: Per gram, the shrew uses 7.4 mL O₂ per hour and the elephant 0.07. The drop is huge from shrew to mouse (7.4 to 1.65) and small from horse to elephant (0.11 to 0.07).
options: The values fall from the smallest mammal to the largest, the opposite of this statement.
This matches both the direction of the trend and its shape.
The steps shrink from left to right (a drop of 5.75 first, then 0.04 at the end), so the drops are not equal.
The values differ about a hundredfold between shrew and elephant.

why.correct: Total use = use per gram × mass = 7.4 mL per g per h × 4 g × 1 h = 29.6 mL.

Endotherms keep warm with heat released by their own cellular respiration. A small body has a lot of surface for its volume, so heat escapes fast relative to mass, and each gram must burn more fuel, using more oxygen, to replace it.
options: This links small size to a high surface area ÷ volume, fast heat loss, and more respiration per gram to replace the heat.
Shrew and elephant cells are about the same size; the difference is in the whole body's surface and volume.
Holding less heat means losing it faster for its mass, so a small endotherm needs more oxygen per gram to stay warm, not less.
Taking in oxygen slowly would limit its oxygen use, not raise it; the high use reflects high demand.

why.correct: Total use = per-gram use × mass. Elephant: 0.07 × 3,800,000 g ≈ 266,000 mL per hour. Mouse: 1.65 × 25 g ≈ 41 mL per hour. Each gram of elephant uses less, but the whole elephant uses thousands of times more.
options: The bars compare use per gram, not per animal, so their heights do not show total use.
A lower surface area ÷ volume lowers the need per gram; total need still grows with body mass.
Per-gram values must be multiplied by mass to compare whole animals, and the elephant's total is far larger.
The elephant's per-gram value (0.07) is lower than the mouse's (1.65), so this reason is false.

why.correct: An ectotherm's body temperature follows its surroundings; it does not burn extra fuel to stay warm. So at rest it uses far less oxygen per gram than an endotherm of the same mass.
options: The mouse burns fuel to replace lost heat; the lizard does not, so its oxygen use per gram is much lower.
Same mass gives a similar surface area ÷ volume, but only the mouse spends energy keeping warm.
Losing heat costs an ectotherm no extra oxygen, because it does not replace that heat from its own respiration.
Scales do not change body shape much, and the lizard does not spend oxygen replacing lost heat anyway.

why.correct: Surface area = 4πr², so doubling r multiplies it by 2² = 4. Volume = 4/3 πr³, so it is multiplied by 2³ = 8. The ratio is multiplied by 4 ÷ 8 = ½.
options: Both grow, but volume grows faster, so the ratio falls, not rises.
Keeping the shape keeps proportions, but surface area and volume still scale differently with size.
4 times the surface over 8 times the volume gives half the ratio.
Volume rises 8 times and surface 4 times, so the ratio halves; it does not drop to a quarter.

why.correct: Surface area = 4 × 3.14 × 25 = 314 µm²; volume = 4/3 × 3.14 × 125 = 524 µm³. 314 ÷ 524 = 0.6 per µm. (For any sphere the ratio simplifies to 3 ÷ r.)
Root hairs and microvilli are thin projections that add a lot of membrane without adding much volume. The other changes lower the surface for exchange or make the path longer.
options: Each root hair is a long, thin outgrowth of one cell, adding surface for taking in water and minerals.
Larger, rounder cells have a lower surface area ÷ volume, so they exchange less per unit of volume.
Microvilli are tiny finger-like folds of the cell membrane that multiply the surface for absorbing food molecules.
A thicker layer does not add surface; it lengthens the distance gases must travel, slowing exchange.
Merging many small alveoli into fewer large ones lowers the total surface for gas exchange.

why.correct: Many small alveoli have far more total surface than a few large ones holding the same air. Losing that surface means less oxygen can diffuse into the blood per breath.
options: Larger sacs hold air but have less total surface, and exchange happens across surface, not volume.
Fewer, larger sacs give less total surface, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood each breath.
The volume of air can stay similar while the surface for exchange shrinks, so exchange slows.
Larger sacs still have walls that oxygen crosses; there is less surface, not none.

why.correct: Materials enter and wastes leave across the surface, but every part of the volume uses materials and makes wastes. As a cell grows, volume outpaces surface, and the center lies farther from the surface, so diffusion cannot keep up.
options: Demand rises with volume; supply rises with surface; volume wins as size increases.
Cells make new phospholipids as they grow; membrane supply is not the limit.
Per unit of volume, a larger cell takes in materials more slowly, not faster.
DNA works the same in large and small cells; the limit is exchange across the surface.

why.correct: Doubling each side multiplies surface by 4 and volume by 8, so the ratio halves. The membrane itself is no thicker, so crossing it takes the same time.

variables.name: Surface area of the cell
variables.why: Surface area is 6 × side², so it rises from 600 µm² to 2,400 µm², four times as much.

variables.name: Surface area ÷ volume
variables.why: Volume rises eightfold (1,000 to 8,000 µm³) while surface rises fourfold, so the ratio halves, from 0.6 to 0.3 per µm.

variables.name: Time for oxygen to cross the membrane itself
variables.why: The membrane is the same thickness in a large cell as in a small one, so crossing it takes the same time; what changes is the distance to the cell's center and the surface per unit of volume.

why.correct: A huge animal has a low surface area ÷ volume and loses heat slowly. Large, thin ears with many blood vessels add a lot of exchange surface, and flapping moves air over it, so heat leaves the blood faster.
options: Thin ears add much surface with little volume, speeding heat loss from the blood.
Looking larger does not change how much oxygen the body uses per gram.
The ears are thin flaps of skin and blood vessels, not water stores.
Ears add a little volume, not remove it; their value is the surface they add.

why.correct: Pressed together, the birds act like one larger body with a lower surface area ÷ volume. Each loses heat more slowly, so it needs to release less heat by cellular respiration and uses less oxygen.
options: Huddling birds stay mostly still; the saving in heat loss far outweighs any extra movement.
Less exposed surface means slower heat loss, so less fuel and oxygen are needed to stay warm.
A bird's own shape does not change, but much of its surface now touches warm neighbors instead of cold air.
There is plenty of oxygen in the air around the group; the change is in how much each bird needs.

why.correct: In diffusion, particles move randomly, and more of them happen to move from a crowded region to a sparse one than the reverse, so they spread down their concentration gradient with no energy from the cell.
options: This is diffusion: net spreading down a concentration gradient, driven by random motion.
Moving particles from sparse to crowded needs an energy input; diffusion runs the other way.
Diffusion has no preferred direction toward the center; it follows the concentration gradient.
Particles keep moving all the time; diffusion is the net spreading that results.

why.correct: To test the effect of size, everything else must be held constant. Here soaking time changed along with size, so it is a second variable that could explain the result.
options: Using different agar would add another difference, making the comparison worse, not better.
Time is a second variable that changed with size, so it must be held constant.
Comparing two or more sizes is exactly what the experiment needs; more sizes would be better.
Changing the time in either direction still mixes time with size; it should be the same for both.

why.correct: At 37 °C the share of mixed cells climbs to 92% by 40 minutes; at 15 °C it never passes 4%.
options: This matches both curves: a steep rise at 37 °C and almost none at 15 °C.
Only the 37 °C curve reaches about 50% at 20 minutes; at 15 °C the value is 2%.
At 10 minutes, 24% of cells are mixed at 37 °C and 1% at 15 °C, so mixing is slower in the cold.
By 40 minutes, 92% are mixed at 37 °C and 4% at 15 °C, nowhere near half in either case.

why.correct: Rate = change in value ÷ change in time = (78 − 24) ÷ (30 − 10) = 54 ÷ 20 = 2.7 percentage points per minute.
Phospholipids and many proteins move sideways within a fluid bilayer. Cooling slows the molecules and lets the tails pack closer, so the membrane becomes less fluid and proteins barely move.
options: Moderate cold slows molecules but does not denature proteins, and the labels are still visible at 15 °C.
This links temperature to fluidity and fluidity to sideways movement of proteins.
Making new protein is not needed to explain the mixing, and newly made protein would not carry the labels added before fusion.
The cells were already fused before they were cooled; the halves form one continuous membrane at both temperatures.

why.correct: If mixing still happens when no new protein can be made, the labels must be spreading by movement of proteins already in the membrane. (In the original experiments, blocking protein synthesis did not stop the mixing.)
options: Blocking new protein synthesis tests the skeptic's idea directly: mixing that continues must come from movement.
A longer cold run tests how slow movement is in the cold, not whether new protein causes mixing.
With one color only, mixing could not be seen at all, so the test gives no information.
A middle temperature tests the effect of temperature, which both explanations could account for.

why.correct: Cholesterol is a buffer for fluidity. In the cold, its rigid rings wedge between the phospholipid tails and stop them packing tightly, so the membrane stays more fluid than it would otherwise. (In the heat, it does the opposite, restraining movement.)
options: Cholesterol stiffens the membrane at high temperatures but keeps it more fluid at low temperatures.
In the cold, cholesterol prevents tight packing, so proteins can move a little more.
Cholesterol sits among the tails; it does not bind or block the labeled proteins.
Cholesterol does not produce heat; it changes how tightly the lipids pack.

why.correct: Unsaturated fatty acids fall from 68% to 38% as temperature rises from 15 to 43 °C, but the fluidity index stays between 0.50 and 0.53, with SDs that overlap.
options: The share of unsaturated fatty acids falls, not rises, and fluidity barely changes.
This matches both columns.
Fluidity stays between 0.50 and 0.53; 38 is a percentage of unsaturated fatty acids, not a fluidity value.
The share drops by 30 percentage points, far more than the SDs of 2 to 3.

why.correct: Percent change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100 = (38 − 68) ÷ 68 × 100 = −44.1%, which rounds to −44%.
A double bond puts a bend in a fatty acid tail. Bent tails cannot line up as closely as straight saturated tails, so they stay loosely packed and free to move even in the cold.
options: Unsaturated tails are still hydrocarbon chains and still hydrophobic; water stays out of the bilayer's core.
Kinked tails pack loosely, which keeps the membrane fluid at low temperature.
The difference is the kinks, not the length; longer tails would actually pack more tightly.
Hydrocarbon tails are nonpolar and do not form hydrogen bonds with each other.

why.correct: Normal cells keep their membranes fluid in the cold by raising their share of kinked, unsaturated tails (68% at 15 °C in the table). This strain stays at 45%, so its tails pack more tightly at 15 °C, the membrane stiffens, and the proteins that do the membrane's jobs cannot work properly.
options: Cold slows all tails and lets them pack closer; the normal strain makes up for this by adding unsaturated tails, which this strain cannot do.
Cold makes all tails move less; straight saturated tails pack closer, not farther apart.
Without the option of adding unsaturated tails, the membrane stiffens and its proteins suffer.
Cold does not convert fatty acids, and this strain cannot change its fatty acid mix at any temperature.

why.correct: The claim has two parts, a change in lipids and a steady fluidity. The fluidity column stays nearly constant while the lipid column swings from 68% to 38%, so both parts are supported.
options: This shows both parts of the claim: lipids change while fluidity stays put.
Growing at four temperatures does not show what happened to fluidity.
One value shows the lipid mix at one temperature but says nothing about fluidity staying steady.
Replicates make the data more reliable but are not themselves evidence for the claim.

why.correct: Both sides of the membrane are watery, so the hydrophilic heads face outward on each side and the hydrophobic tails hide from water in the middle.
options: This is the bilayer: tails inside, heads facing water on both faces.
Tails facing water would be pushed together by water, which is exactly why they end up in the middle.
A single layer would leave tails exposed to the watery outside, which is unstable.
Alternating heads and tails would expose tails to water on both faces.

why.correct: The middle of the bilayer is made of hydrophobic tails. A stretch of protein there is stable only if its side chains are nonpolar, too; polar or charged side chains would be pushed toward water.
options: The heads are at the surfaces, not in the middle; charged side chains in the core would be unstable.
Nonpolar side chains match the hydrophobic core, holding the protein in place.
Hydrocarbon tails cannot form hydrogen bonds, and polar side chains are unstable among them.
The hydrophobic core strongly favors nonpolar side chains, so the mix is far from random.

why.correct: A charged side chain is strongly hydrophilic. Buried among hydrophobic tails it is unstable, so the protein tends to fold or insert wrongly, and its job may suffer.
options: Charged side chains are repelled by the nonpolar tails, so the fit gets worse, not better.
A charged group in the hydrophobic core destabilizes the protein's position.
One change in a membrane-crossing stretch does not send a protein to the nucleus.
A single amino acid in the wrong environment can change a protein's shape and position, as with sickle-shaped red blood cells caused by one change in hemoglobin.

why.correct: Membrane proteins move substances across, act as receptors for signals, and (with attached carbohydrates) let cells recognize each other. Instructions are stored in DNA, and the bilayer holds together by hydrophobic interactions, not proteins.
options: Many membrane proteins provide routes for particular substances to cross.
Receptor proteins bind signaling molecules and change what the cell does.
Glycoproteins on the surface act as identity tags that other cells recognize.
Instructions for proteins are stored in DNA in the nucleus, not in membrane proteins.
The tails stay hydrophobic; proteins do not change the chemistry of the lipids.
The two layers are held together by hydrophobic interactions among the tails, not by protein bonds.

why.correct: The sugars are attached on the inner (lumen) side of the ER and Golgi membranes. When a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, its inner face turns outward, so the chains face outside the cell, where they act in recognition.
options: The sugars are added inside the ER and Golgi, not in the cytosol.
Vesicle fusion turns the lumen-facing side of the membrane into the cell's outer surface.
Proteins move sideways freely but almost never flip from one face to the other.
Sugar chains are hydrophilic; they face the watery outside because of where they were added.

why.correct: A molecule that cannot cross the membrane acts by binding a receptor on the cell surface. Only cells with that receptor respond.
options: Receptors make cells responsive; cells without the receptor ignore the signal.
Plasma membranes are about the same thickness in all cells; that is not the difference.
The blood reaches skin and liver alike, so this would not explain a cell-type difference.
Size does not decide a response; the receptor does.

why.correct: At warmer temperatures cholesterol's rigid rings hold neighboring phospholipids back and limit their movement; at low temperatures the same molecules stop the tails from packing tightly. Either way it keeps fluidity within a working range.
options: When warm, cholesterol damps phospholipid movement, so the membrane is not too fluid.
That is cholesterol's effect in the cold relative to a cholesterol-free membrane; in the warm it restrains movement.
Cholesterol sits among the phospholipids; it does not take the place of proteins.
Cholesterol molecules sit within each layer, among the tails, not as a separate layer.

why.correct: Warming makes the lipids move faster, so the bilayer becomes more fluid and proteins slide faster, but it remains a bilayer.

variables.name: Fluidity of the plasma membrane
variables.why: Warmer phospholipids move faster and pack less tightly, so the bilayer becomes more fluid.

variables.name: Speed at which membrane proteins slide sideways
variables.why: In a more fluid bilayer, proteins meet less resistance and slide sideways faster.

variables.name: Number of phospholipid layers in the membrane
variables.why: The membrane stays a bilayer; warming changes how freely its molecules move, not how many layers there are.

why.correct: Peripheral proteins are attached loosely to the surface, often by ionic bonds that salt can break. Integral proteins are embedded in the hydrophobic core, so the bilayer itself must be broken up to free them.
options: A salt wash frees surface-held proteins; only a detergent frees those buried in the bilayer.
This reverses the two: embedded proteins need the bilayer disrupted.
Size does not explain needing a detergent; being embedded in the bilayer does.
Length does not decide this; a protein freed by salt alone is not embedded.

why.correct: "Fluid" means the phospholipids and many proteins slide sideways within the layer; "mosaic" means the membrane is a patchwork of many kinds of proteins set in the lipids.
options: This is the model: a fluid lipid bilayer with a patchwork of proteins.
Older models put protein sheets on a lipid layer; the fluid mosaic model has proteins set in the bilayer, and no water layer in the middle.
Mosaic means a patchwork, but the pieces are not fixed; they move.
The membrane is not flowing away; its molecules move within it while it stays in place.

why.correct: Permeability falls from nonpolar (CO₂, 10⁻¹) through uncharged polar molecules (10⁻³ to 10⁻¹⁰, slower as they get bigger) to ions (10⁻¹¹ and 10⁻¹²).
options: Sodium (23 g/mol) and chloride (35.5 g/mol) are small but the slowest of all, so charge matters more than size.
This ordering follows polarity and charge, with size mattering within the polar group.
The ions (10⁻¹¹ and 10⁻¹²) are slower than water (10⁻³), a polar molecule of similar size.
Urea and glycerol (60 and 92 g/mol) cross at 10⁻⁶ cm/s, a million times faster than the ions.

why.correct: Divide the two values: 10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻¹⁰ = 10⁻³⁻⁽⁻¹⁰⁾ = 10⁷. Water crosses about ten million times faster than glucose.
Sodium is far smaller than glucose yet crosses about a hundred times more slowly (10⁻¹² against 10⁻¹⁰), so something besides size, its charge, controls crossing.
options: Here too the larger molecule is slower, which fits the claim instead of refuting it.
A tiny ion crossing slower than a large sugar shows that size is not the only factor.
Here the larger molecule is slower, which fits the size claim rather than refuting it.
The smaller molecule is faster here, which fits the claim.

why.correct: Ions carry a full charge and are surrounded by a shell of attracted water molecules. Leaving that water to enter the hydrophobic middle of the bilayer takes a lot of energy, so they almost never do.
options: Charge, not mass, is what keeps ions out of the hydrophobic core.
Sodium (23 g/mol) is lighter than urea (60 g/mol) and glycerol (92 g/mol), which cross about a million times faster, so mass is not the reason.
Charged ions are repelled by the nonpolar tails; they do not bind to them.
Ions are not chemically changed by the heads; they simply stay out of the core.

why.correct: Glucose crosses a bare bilayer about a billion times (10⁹) more slowly than CO₂. Fast uptake needs a transport protein that gives glucose a hydrophilic route across.
options: A thicker hydrophobic layer would slow glucose further, not help it cross.
A transport protein gives a polar molecule like glucose a route that avoids the hydrophobic core.
Every plasma membrane is a full bilayer; removing phospholipids would break it, not speed glucose.
Cholesterol is part of the hydrophobic region and does not attract polar glucose.

why.correct: In 3 minutes the aquaporin oocytes grew by 36%, the controls by 3%, and the mercury-treated aquaporin oocytes by 9%.
options: At 3 minutes the volumes are 1.36, 1.09 and 1.03, so the paces clearly differ.
This matches the three curves.
Mercury-treated aquaporin oocytes swelled more slowly (1.09 at 3 minutes) than untreated ones (1.36).
The controls swelled slowest; the injected water was a tiny volume added three days earlier.

why.correct: Rate = change in volume ÷ change in time = (1.36 − 1.00) ÷ 3 min = 0.12 per minute, twelve times the control's 0.01 per minute.
The injection could damage the membrane or add water. Giving the control the same injection, minus the mRNA, leaves the mRNA as the only difference between the groups.
options: Matching the injection isolates the mRNA as the one variable that differs.
The control is meant to show the normal, slow swelling, not to match the aquaporin group.
Plain water carries no mRNA, so the controls make no added aquaporin.
The injected volume is tiny; starting sizes are matched, and volumes are given relative to the start.

why.correct: mRNA is read by ribosomes to build a protein. The aquaporin made this way was sent to the plasma membrane, where it gave water a fast route through the bilayer.
options: A small amount of mRNA barely changes how concentrated the contents are; the controls got the same volume of liquid and swelled slowly.
This links the mRNA to a protein, the protein to the membrane, and the membrane to faster water entry.
mRNA is read by ribosomes in the cytoplasm; it is not built into the membrane.
mRNA does not digest lipids, and mercury, which binds aquaporin, slowed the swelling, pointing to the protein.

why.correct: The aquaporin group swelled twelve times as fast as the controls, a difference far beyond the small spread expected among 8 oocytes, and mercury reduced it. The data are inconsistent with "no effect".
options: Some slow swelling in controls is expected; the question is whether aquaporin changes the pace, and it clearly does.
Both the large difference and the mercury result point to an effect of aquaporin.
The mercury group is a little faster than the controls, but that alone is weak evidence; the main evidence is the much faster swelling with working aquaporin.
Bursting early is itself a result of very fast water entry, which argues against the null hypothesis.

why.correct: With penicillin, 12% of cells stayed intact in dilute medium but 91% in sucrose medium. Without penicillin, about 98 to 99% stayed intact in both.
options: In sucrose medium 91% of penicillin-treated cells were intact, so most survived there.
This matches the table: penicillin's effect depends on the medium.
Without penicillin, 98% of cells in sucrose medium were intact, so sucrose itself did little harm.
Penicillin in dilute medium cut intact cells from 99% to 12%.

why.correct: A bacterium's contents are more concentrated than a dilute medium, so water moves in and the cell presses outward. The cell wall resists that push. With the wall weakened, cells in dilute medium burst; in a medium as concentrated as their contents, little water enters, so they survive but lose their rod shape.
options: This links the wall's job, resisting the outward push of entering water, to the four results.
Penicillin acts on the wall, not the membrane; the round, intact cells in sucrose show the membrane is fine.
If sucrose let cells destroy penicillin, they would keep their rod shape; instead they turned round, showing the wall was still weakened.
Penicillin targets wall building; the difference between media is about water entering, not about penicillin entering.

why.correct: Without this group, you could not tell whether sucrose itself changes survival. It shows that sucrose alone leaves 98% of cells intact, so the comparison with penicillin is fair.
options: This control separates the effect of sucrose from the effect of penicillin.
Without penicillin in it, this group cannot change how penicillin works.
Each condition already has three cultures; the group's purpose is comparison, not numbers.
Cells in sucrose without penicillin stay rod-shaped, so sucrose alone does not round them; only the cells with weakened walls turn round.

why.correct: Penicillin blocks the building of peptidoglycan, a wall material found in bacteria. Animal cells have no wall at all, so the drug's target is missing.
options: No peptidoglycan in human cells means penicillin's target is absent.
Animal cells have no cell wall of any kind; cellulose walls belong to plants.
Body fluids are close in concentration to cells' contents, but that is not why penicillin spares human cells; they simply lack its target.
Penicillin circulates in the body for hours; it spares human cells because they lack its target, not because they destroy it.

why.correct: Ions and large polar molecules such as glucose are kept out by the hydrophobic core. Small nonpolar molecules and lipid-soluble ones such as steroids dissolve through the bilayer by simple diffusion.
options: As an ion, K⁺ is repelled by the hydrophobic core and needs a transport protein.
O₂ is small and nonpolar, so it crosses the bilayer directly.
Glucose is large and polar, so it needs a transport protein to cross quickly.
CO₂ is small and nonpolar and crosses the bilayer directly.
Steroids are lipids, so they dissolve through the hydrophobic core without help.
N₂ is small and nonpolar and crosses the bilayer directly.

why.correct: Steroids are lipids with fused carbon rings, so they dissolve through the hydrophobic core. Insulin is a large, polar protein that the bilayer keeps out, so its receptor must face outside.
options: Steroids are uncharged and lipid-like; charged molecules are the ones the bilayer keeps out.
Being a lipid lets estrogen cross; being large and polar keeps insulin outside.
Aquaporins let water through, not hormones.
Hormones like estrogen are made in one organ and carried in the blood to cells elsewhere, so they must cross membranes.

why.correct: The plant cell's wall is strong and resists stretching, so as the cell swells the wall presses back until water stops entering. An animal cell has no wall to stop the swelling.
options: The plant cell's wall resists the swelling, so it does not burst.
The wall protects the plant cell from bursting; the animal cell has no such protection.
Cholesterol affects membrane fluidity, not resistance to swelling; and it is the plant cell that has the wall.
Water does cross membranes, a little through the bilayer and much more through aquaporins.

why.correct: Aquaporins speed up water only. Small nonpolar gases cross through the bilayer itself, so blocking aquaporins slows water but leaves the gases unchanged.

variables.name: Rate at which water crosses the plasma membrane
variables.why: Most water crosses through aquaporins; with them blocked, water can cross only slowly through the bilayer itself.

variables.name: Rate at which oxygen crosses the plasma membrane
variables.why: Oxygen is small and nonpolar and crosses directly through the bilayer, not through aquaporins, so blocking them does not change it.

variables.name: Rate at which carbon dioxide crosses the plasma membrane
variables.why: Carbon dioxide is also small and nonpolar and diffuses straight through the bilayer, so it is unaffected.

why.correct: Selective permeability means the bilayer and its proteins let some substances through and hold others back, so the cell can keep its contents different from its surroundings.
options: Selective permeability explains both parts: oxygen passes, proteins and glucose stay in.
Oxygen crosses freely, so the membrane is not shut to everything but water.
Molecules in solution move constantly whatever their mass; they stay in because the membrane holds them back.
The membrane's permeability does not switch from open to shut in this way.

why.correct: Plant walls are mostly cellulose, fungal walls chitin, and bacterial walls peptidoglycan (a mesh of sugars cross-linked by short chains of amino acids).
options: Each group is matched with its wall material.
Chitin is the fungal wall material (and insects' outer skeleton); cellulose is the plant one.
Peptidoglycan is found in bacteria, not plants.
Fungi use chitin, and peptidoglycan belongs to bacteria.

why.correct: Iodine was concentrated in the beaker and absent from the bag, so it diffused in and met the starch. Starch molecules are too large for the tubing's pores, so they stayed in the bag and none reached the beaker.
options: Starch cannot pass the tubing's pores; if it had left, the beaker would have turned blue-black.
Iodine moved in down its gradient and starch stayed put, so the color appeared only inside.
Tubing is a plastic film; it has no proteins or ATP, so the movement was passive.
Iodine and glucose diffuse independently, each down its own gradient; glucose moving out cannot carry iodine in.

why.correct: Glucose diffuses out until its concentration is the same on both sides. Molecules keep moving at random, so they still cross both ways, but equal numbers cross each way, so there is no net change: a dynamic equilibrium.
options: Diffusion evens out concentrations; it does not move every molecule to one side.
This describes dynamic equilibrium: equal concentrations, crossings still happening at equal rates both ways.
Molecules keep moving and crossing at equilibrium; only the net movement stops.
Passive movement cannot build up a higher concentration on one side; that would need energy.

why.correct: Glucose moved from the bag (high) to the beaker (none), and iodine from the beaker (high) to the bag (none). Each went down its gradient, driven by its own motion, which is passive transport.
options: Each substance moved from high to low concentration with no energy supplied, which is passive transport.
Opposite directions just mean the two gradients pointed opposite ways; each move was still downhill.
There are no vesicles in tubing; the molecules passed through pores one by one.
Passive movement continues for as long as a gradient exists; time alone does not make it active.

why.correct: Tubing is a sieve: whatever fits the pores passes. A plasma membrane is a hydrophobic bilayer, so small ions are blocked while nonpolar molecules pass, and its transport proteins let particular substances through, some using energy.
options: This names the real difference: size-based pores against chemistry plus specific proteins.
Both are selectively permeable; a plasma membrane is very selective.
Water crosses plasma membranes, through the bilayer and especially through aquaporins.
Glucose reached the beaker within 30 minutes, so diffusion through the tubing is not that slow.

why.correct: The untreated cells reach a ratio of 9.6 by 60 minutes; the cyanide-treated cells rise to 1.0 by 30 minutes and stay there.
options: The cyanide batch never goes above 1.0, so only the untreated batch accumulates the amino acid.
This matches both curves.
At every time point the cyanide batch is below the untreated batch, so its uptake is slower.
The ratio of 1.0 is where the cyanide batch levels off; the untreated batch keeps rising past 9.

why.correct: A ratio above 1.0 means the amino acid is moving from low to high concentration, which takes energy. When cyanide stops ATP production, the cells can still take it in passively, but only until inside equals outside.
options: If the bilayer were leaky, the ratio would not climb neatly to 1.0 and hold; the pattern fits passive movement to equal concentrations.
This links the ratio above 1.0 to active transport and ATP, and the level at 1.0 to passive transport.
Cyanide stops ATP production in the cells; it does not change the amino acid outside.
The measured amino acid is the labeled one from the medium, so cells making their own would not raise its value.

why.correct: The untreated range runs from 1.8 to 2.4 and the cyanide range from 0.5 to 0.7. Error bars of ±2 SE that do not overlap suggest the difference is statistically significant, not just sampling noise.
options: Non-overlapping ±2 SE bars are evidence of a real difference.
The ranges (1.8 to 2.4 and 0.5 to 0.7) do not overlap at all.
Non-overlapping bars point to a difference, not the absence of one.
Error bars can be compared at any time point where both means have them.

why.correct: Inside ÷ outside = 9.6, so inside = 9.6 × 0.50 mM = 4.8 mM.
With no new ATP, active transport stops. The amino acid is far more concentrated inside, so it slowly moves out down its gradient until inside and outside are about equal.
options: A steep gradient now points outward, and nothing is moving the amino acid back in, so it leaks out.
Cells hold only a small amount of ATP, used up within minutes once production stops.
Without ATP the gradient is no longer maintained, so the ratio falls toward equal.
Cyanide stops ATP production; it does not destroy amino acids, and passive leakage is gradual.

why.correct: At 37 °C healthy cells had 310 ng of LDL inside, against 12 ng for cells lacking the receptor: 310 ÷ 12 ≈ 26, about 25 times as much.
options: 310 against 12 ng is a large difference, not about the same.
This matches the inside-the-cell column at 37 °C.
Receptor-lacking cells bound 5 ng, against 40 ng for healthy cells.
Healthy cells bound 120 ng at 4 °C and 40 ng at 37 °C, so binding was lower at 37 °C.

why.correct: Binding to a receptor needs no work from the cell, so it happens in the cold. Taking the bound LDL in needs the membrane to fold inward and pinch off a vesicle, which stops at 4 °C. So LDL piles up on the surface.
options: Healthy cells bound 120 ng at 4 °C against 6 ng for receptor-lacking cells, so the receptors are clearly working.
This separates binding (still works) from endocytosis (stops in the cold).
LDL particles are far too large to diffuse through a bilayer.
There is no evidence of LDL being pushed out; it is bound but not taken in.

why.correct: Cells clear LDL from the blood by binding it to receptors and taking it in. Without working receptors, LDL builds up in the blood. (This is what happens in an inherited disease that causes very high blood cholesterol and early heart disease.)
options: Receptor-lacking cells took in only 12 ng against 310 for healthy cells, so they are slower, not faster.
Less removal by cells means more LDL stays in the blood.
LDL particles are far too large to cross membranes by diffusion.
Nothing in the data suggests LDL breaks down on its own in the blood; it is cleared by cells.

why.correct: In the cold, receptors still bind LDL but endocytosis stops. Comparing 4 °C with 37 °C shows the receptors work at the surface first and that the uptake step is a separate, energy-using process.
options: The 4 °C data show binding without uptake, isolating the two steps.
Cold slows the cells without killing them; they still bind LDL.
The 4 °C cultures test a different condition; they are not extra replicates of 37 °C.
The LDL is supplied, labeled, by the researchers; the cells do not make it.

why.correct: Only oxygen moving from the air sacs into the blood goes down its gradient with no energy from the cell. The other three need energy: engulfing and releasing in vesicles are bulk transport, and taking in potassium against its gradient is active transport.
options: Oxygen is more concentrated in the air sacs than in the blood arriving there, so it diffuses in.
Engulfing a bacterium is endocytosis (phagocytosis), which uses energy to reshape the membrane.
Releasing insulin from vesicles is exocytosis, a form of bulk transport that uses energy.
Moving potassium from low to high concentration is active transport and needs ATP.

why.correct: Building up a concentration 100 times higher inside means moving potassium from low to high concentration, against its gradient, which needs energy from ATP.
options: Diffusion moves particles from high to low, so it could never build up a higher concentration inside.
Moving ions against a steep gradient is active transport.
Exocytosis releases material from a cell; it does not take anything in.
Aquaporins let water through, not ions, and water flow could not concentrate potassium.

why.correct: In exocytosis the vesicle's membrane becomes part of the plasma membrane. Normally endocytosis takes membrane back in at a similar pace. With endocytosis blocked, membrane is added but not removed, so the surface grows.
options: Fusion adds vesicle membrane to the cell surface, and blocked endocytosis cannot take it back.
Removing membrane in vesicles is endocytosis, which is blocked here.
Releasing contents by exocytosis requires the vesicle to fuse with the plasma membrane.
Fused vesicle membrane joins the bilayer sideways; the membrane stays one bilayer thick.

why.correct: Pinocytosis ("cell drinking") takes in droplets of extracellular fluid in small vesicles, without choosing particular molecules.
options: Pinocytosis is the non-selective uptake of fluid in small vesicles.
Phagocytosis ("cell eating") engulfs large particles, such as bacteria, in large vesicles.
Exocytosis releases material from the cell; it does not take fluid in.
Simple diffusion moves single molecules through the bilayer, with no vesicles.

why.correct: Without ATP, active transport and bulk transport slow and stop, while passive transport such as the diffusion of oxygen continues.

variables.name: Active transport of ions into the cell
variables.why: Active transport moves substances against their gradient using energy from ATP; once the cell's small ATP store is used up, it slows and stops.

variables.name: Diffusion of oxygen into the cell
variables.why: Oxygen crosses by simple diffusion, driven by its own motion down its gradient, so it needs no ATP and is not directly affected.

variables.name: Exocytosis of secretory vesicles
variables.why: Moving vesicles to the membrane and fusing them uses energy from ATP, so release slows.

why.correct: Selective permeability slows ion leaks, and active transport, powered by ATP, keeps moving K⁺ in and Na⁺ out. Together they maintain an internal environment different from the outside. Stop the ATP and the differences slowly run down toward equal.
options: Ions do leak across slowly, so the differences would fade without continual work.
Slow leaks plus continual active transport keep the inside different from the outside.
Keeping the concentrations unequal takes energy; without ATP they slowly even out.
Diffusion moves particles from high to low, so it erases differences rather than creating them.

why.correct: In passive transport the cell spends no ATP. The particles move because they already have kinetic energy, and random motion spreads them down their gradient.
options: Passive transport uses no ATP; that is what makes it passive.
The energy is the particles' own kinetic energy, not the cell's.
The membrane stays intact; nothing about passive transport breaks it down.
Particles move by their own thermal motion; the cell does not direct heat to push them.

why.correct: Glucose uptake gains 6.0 nmol/min over the first 2 mM but only 0.8 nmol/min over the last 5 mM: the curve flattens toward a ceiling.
options: Correct: the first 2 mM add 6.0 nmol/min, while going from 15 to 20 mM adds only 0.8 nmol/min.
That describes substance X, whose rate climbs 1.0 nmol/min for every 2 mM. Glucose gains less with each step.
The pattern is the reverse: the steep part is at low concentrations and the curve flattens at high ones.
The rate never falls; it keeps creeping up, from 12.9 at 10 mM to 15.0 at 20 mM.

why.correct: A curve that levels off is the signature of a fixed number of transport proteins: once every carrier is busy, adding more glucose cannot speed transport. A straight line means rate tracks the gradient, as in simple diffusion through the bilayer.
options: Correct: a fixed number of carriers caps the rate, while diffusion through the bilayer has no such cap and stays proportional to the gradient.
Nothing was inside the cells at the start, so glucose was moving down its gradient: no pump is needed. Glucose enters red blood cells by facilitated diffusion.
Size does not change with concentration. A molecule either can or cannot cross the bilayer; glucose cannot at any concentration and needs a carrier throughout.
Glucose molecules dissolve and move independently in water; the leveling off comes from the limited number of carriers, not from clumping.

why.correct: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (15.0 − 12.9) ÷ 12.9 × 100 ≈ 16%. Doubling the concentration raised the rate by only about a sixth, because nearly every carrier was already busy at 10 mM. For substance X the same doubling raises the rate by 100%.
The ceiling of the glucose curve is set by how many carriers there are. Halve the carriers and the top rate halves. X does not use the carriers, so its line is unchanged.
options: Correct: with half the carriers, the most glucose they can move per minute is about half as much, and X's route through the bilayer is untouched.
Blocking carriers lowers the ceiling. A shift to higher concentration with the same ceiling would come from something competing with glucose for the same carriers, not from losing carriers.
X crosses the lipid bilayer directly, so blocking glucose carriers has no effect on it.
Fewer carriers fill up sooner, not later; the glucose curve still levels off, just at a lower rate.

why.correct: Carriers are specific: they bind molecules of a particular shape. If a look-alike molecule slows X's uptake, the two are competing for the same binding sites, which a bilayer route would not show.
options: Correct: competition for a binding site is evidence for a specific transport protein, because diffusion through the bilayer has no site to compete for.
Lower temperature slows nearly all movement of molecules, including simple diffusion, so it cannot tell the two routes apart.
This repeats the original pattern, which is exactly what simple diffusion predicts; it adds no evidence for a carrier.
This shows only that X does not share the glucose carrier. X could still diffuse through the bilayer or use some other carrier.

why.correct: Na⁺ is 145 mM outside and 12 mM inside, so its gradient points inward. With the pump stopped, Na⁺ leaking in is no longer removed, and the inside concentration climbs.
options: Correct: Na⁺ moved from 145 mM outside toward 12 mM inside, from crowded to scarce.
K⁺ did leave, which is down its gradient, but the reason given is wrong: K⁺ is more concentrated inside (140 mM) than outside (4 mM).
Na⁺ is more concentrated outside, not inside. The outside value stayed flat because the dish holds far more fluid than the cells.
K⁺ moved out of the cells, not in; the inside value fell. The outside value barely moved because the dish is so large.

why.correct: Outside ÷ inside = 145 mM ÷ 12 mM ≈ 12.1. The pump keeps Na⁺ about twelve times more concentrated outside, a steep gradient that stores energy.
Before ouabain, the inside Na⁺ level was steady because the pump removed Na⁺ as fast as it leaked in. Stopping the pump removes the outflow while the leak continues, so Na⁺ builds up inside.
options: Correct: a steady level is a balance of leak in and pumping out; remove the pumping and the leak wins.
The description says ouabain binds the pump and stops it. No extra channels are needed to explain the data: the normal leak is enough.
Na⁺ is an element's ion; cells cannot make it from other molecules. It can only come in from outside.
A stopped pump does not reverse. The extra Na⁺ comes in passively through channels, down its gradient.

why.correct: With the pump stopped, nothing rebuilds the gradients. Ions keep moving down their gradients until the inside and outside become more alike, and the stored charge difference shrinks.

variables.name: Na⁺ inside the cell
variables.why: Na⁺ keeps leaking in down its gradient with nothing removing it, so the inside level keeps rising toward the outside level.

variables.name: K⁺ inside the cell
variables.why: K⁺ keeps leaking out down its gradient, and the stopped pump no longer brings it back in.

variables.name: Na⁺ outside the cell
variables.why: The dish holds far more fluid than the cells, so the small amount of Na⁺ moving into the cells does not change the outside concentration measurably.

variables.name: Size of the charge difference across the membrane (how far from zero)
variables.why: As the Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients run down, less charge separation can be kept up, so the membrane potential moves further toward 0 mV, continuing the trend from −70 to −52 mV.

why.correct: Only the pump moves an ion against its gradient, so only the pump needs ATP. The channels, aquaporins and the glucose carrier all let substances move down their gradients.
options: The pump moves Na⁺ from 12 mM inside to 145 mM outside, against its gradient, and spends ATP to do it.
Na⁺ entering moves from 145 mM to 12 mM, down its gradient, through a channel: passive.
K⁺ leaving moves from 140 mM to 4 mM, down its gradient: passive.
Water moving through aquaporins follows its own gradient and uses no ATP.
A glucose carrier moves glucose from where it is more concentrated to where it is less concentrated: facilitated diffusion, no ATP.

why.correct: A channel is an open tunnel the substance passes through. A carrier grips the substance, changes shape and lets it go on the other side.
options: Correct: binding plus a change of shape is what makes a protein a carrier.
Carriers in facilitated diffusion move substances down their gradient, from high to low, just as channels do.
Carriers in facilitated diffusion use no ATP; the gradient drives the movement. A protein that spends ATP is a pump.
Both are specific. A carrier binds only molecules that fit its binding site; a channel's size and charged lining admit only certain ions.

why.correct: A little water slips through the bilayer, but aquaporins let it cross far faster. Without them, water movement drops sharply but does not fall to zero.
options: Correct: aquaporins speed water across; without them only the slow route through the bilayer is left.
Small amounts of water still slip between the phospholipids, so movement slows rather than stopping.
Cells have no pumps for water molecules. Water moves passively, following its own gradient.
Diffusion still happens, but the aquaporin is the fast route. Losing it is why these people produce large volumes of dilute urine.

why.correct: A voltage-gated Na⁺ channel opens when the membrane voltage changes, letting Na⁺ rush in down its electrochemical gradient. That inrush is the nerve signal. Plugging the channel stops it.
options: Correct: the gated channel is the only fast route for Na⁺; blocked, it cannot open when the voltage changes, so the signal fails.
Pumping out uses the sodium-potassium pump, a different protein. Tetrodotoxin blocks channels, not the pump.
A plugged channel lets nothing through, so Na⁺ entry falls.
Channels are specific: K⁺ moves through its own potassium channels, which tetrodotoxin does not block.

why.correct: Na⁺ is crowded outside, so diffusion favors entry. It is also positive, and opposite charges attract, so the negative inside draws it in too. Both parts of the gradient point inward, which is why Na⁺ rushes in when a channel opens.
options: Correct: concentration and charge both favor Na⁺ entering, a steep inward electrochemical gradient.
A negative inside attracts a positive ion; it pulls Na⁺ in, it does not push it out.
The forces add rather than cancel, and Na⁺ enters through channels without a pump. The pump moves Na⁺ out.
Charge acts on every ion: a positive ion is drawn toward negative regions and a negative ion toward positive ones.

why.correct: Each cycle moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, a net of 1 positive charge out. 100 cycles × 1 = 100 more positive charges out than in each second, which adds a little to the negative charge inside.

Na⁺ binds on the inside; the phosphate from ATP changes the pump's shape so it opens outward and lets Na⁺ go; K⁺ binds from outside; losing the phosphate snaps the pump back, delivering K⁺ inside. The energy from ATP is spent on the shape change that carries ions uphill.
Facilitated diffusion only moves glucose down its gradient. Converting glucose as it arrives stops it from building up inside, so the outside stays higher and net movement inward goes on.
options: Correct: removing glucose on the inside keeps the gradient pointing inward, so passive uptake continues.
The changed molecule is no longer glucose, so it does not occupy the glucose carrier; the carrier keeps working.
A passive carrier gets no energy from chemical changes inside the cell; the glucose still moves down its gradient, not against it.
Carrier transport depends on the gradient: net movement stops when the inside and outside concentrations become equal.

why.correct: What separates facilitated diffusion from active transport is energy and direction. Uptake without ATP, ending when the concentrations are equal, shows the movement is passive and only goes down the gradient.
options: Correct: no ATP needed, and no movement against the gradient. Both point to facilitated diffusion.
Leveling off shows a limited number of transport proteins, but pumps level off too, so it cannot separate the two.
This shows Z needs a protein, but both facilitated diffusion and active transport use proteins.
This again shows the protein is needed, which is true of both mechanisms; it says nothing about energy or direction.

why.correct: The hydrophobic middle of the bilayer blocks charged particles, so ions need a channel or carrier. Small nonpolar molecules dissolve in the bilayer and slip straight across.
options: K⁺ is charged, so the hydrophobic core of the bilayer repels it; it crosses through potassium channels.
O₂ is small and nonpolar and crosses the bilayer directly by simple diffusion.
CO₂ is small and crosses the bilayer directly by simple diffusion.
Steroids are lipids, so they dissolve in the bilayer and cross without a transport protein.

why.correct: A gate decides when a channel is open. The ions still move down their gradient once it opens; the gate ties that movement to the arrival of a signal.
options: Correct: the gate turns the flow on only when the signaling molecule binds.
Gated channels are still passive: Na⁺ flows in down its gradient. No energy is added.
A gate does not add channels; it closes the existing ones most of the time.
A closed channel lets nothing through, and a gate does not change which ions the channel admits when it opens.

why.correct: The potato line crosses 0% between 0.2 mol/L (+7.6%) and 0.4 mol/L (−2.4%). It falls 10 points over that 0.2 mol/L step, so it reaches zero about three-quarters of the way along, near 0.35 mol/L.
options: At 0.2 mol/L the potato cores still gained 7.6% in mass, so water was still moving in.
Correct: interpolating between +7.6% at 0.2 mol/L and −2.4% at 0.4 mol/L puts the zero crossing near 0.35 mol/L.
That is where the sweet potato line crosses zero, not the potato line.
By 0.75 mol/L the potato cores were losing well over 15% of their mass.

why.correct: Plain water in an open beaker has a water potential of 0. The cells hold dissolved solutes, so their water potential is negative. Water moves from higher to lower water potential, into the cells.
options: Correct: solutes inside make the cells' water potential negative, below the 0 of pure water, so water moves in.
Water moves from higher to lower water potential. If the cells' water potential were higher, water would leave them.
Mass rose, so water came in; losing sugar would lower mass. The mass change is driven by osmosis, not sugar loss.
Cells have no pumps for water. Water crosses passively, following water potential.

why.correct: The mean change at 0.8 mol/L is −18.6%, so the core keeps 100 − 18.6 = 81.4% of its mass: 3.20 g × 0.814 = 2.60 g.

Each tissue shows no change where the outside solution matches its own water potential. Sweet potato balances at about 0.50 mol/L, potato at about 0.35 mol/L. A stronger balancing solution means more solute inside the cells and a lower (more negative) water potential.
options: Correct: sweet potato's zero point is at a higher sucrose concentration, so its cells hold more solute and have the lower water potential.
Gaining more mass in water means water was drawn in more strongly, which points to a lower water potential inside, not a higher one.
The error bars do not overlap at 0.2, 0.4 or 0.6 mol/L, where the means differ by 4.8 to 7.8 points.
Potato loses more mass because its cells have less solute, so a given sucrose solution is more strongly hypertonic to them.

why.correct: A large core gains or loses more grams than a small one in the same solution. Dividing by the starting mass puts every core on the same scale.
options: Correct: dividing by starting mass corrects for small differences in core size.
Random error is reduced by repeating trials (here, five cores), not by how the result is expressed.
A change in grams can be negative too: a core that loses 0.4 g has a change of −0.4 g.
Both measures track the same thing, water gained or lost; neither measures water potential or sucrose directly.

why.correct: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp = (−9) + (+3) = −6 bars. The solutes pull the value down; the pressure inside the wall pushes it back up.
Water potentials: A = −5, B = −6, C = −2 bars. Water moves from higher to lower: C (−2) to A (−5) to B (−6).
options: Correct: C has the highest water potential (−2 bars) and B the lowest (−6 bars), with A in between.
This follows solute potential alone. Cell B's Ψs is the most negative, but water moves toward lower total Ψ, so it moves into B, not out of it.
A (−5 bars) is lower than C (−2 bars), so water moves from C into A, not the reverse.
B has the lowest water potential, so water moves into B; it cannot move from B to A.

why.correct: Cell A's water potential is −5 bars, higher than the solution's −10 bars, so water leaves. As the cell shrinks, the push on the wall drops to zero; with more water loss, the contents pull away from the wall (plasmolysis).
options: Correct: water flows from the cell (−5 bars) to the solution (−10 bars); turgor is lost and plasmolysis can follow.
Water enters only when the outside water potential is higher than the cell's. Here it is lower.
Compare total water potentials (−5 against −10 bars), not solute potential alone; a 5-bar difference drives water out.
The membrane holds the cell's solutes in; it is water that crosses. Losing water actually makes the remaining solutes more concentrated.

why.correct: Pure water (Ψ = 0) is higher than the cell (Ψ = −2 bars), so water enters until rising pressure inside the wall brings the cell's water potential up to 0.

variables.name: Pressure potential of cell C
variables.why: Water enters (pure water is at 0 bars, the cell at −2), the contents swell against the wall, and the wall pushes back harder, raising Ψp.

variables.name: Water potential of cell C
variables.why: Water keeps entering until the cell's water potential matches the beaker's, 0 bars, up from −2 bars.

variables.name: Amount of solute inside cell C
variables.why: The membrane keeps the cell's solutes in and only water crosses, so the amount of solute stays the same (its concentration falls a little as water dilutes it).

variables.name: Volume of cell C
variables.why: Water moves in, so the cell swells slightly until the wall stops it.

why.correct: Work out each cell's Ψ (A −5, B −6, C −2 bars), then test each statement against those numbers.
options: C is −2 bars, higher than A (−5) and B (−6).
−4 bars is higher than cell B's −6 bars, so water would enter B from this solution: the solution is hypotonic to B.
A's pressure potential is +2 bars, so its contents still press on the wall: it is turgid, not plasmolyzed. Every living cell has a negative solute potential.
More solute lowers B's water potential, so water moves into B, not out of it.
B's pressure potential is +3 bars; A's, at +2 bars, is the lowest.

why.correct: Distilled water has no solutes, so it is hypotonic to the cells. Water enters, and with no wall to resist the swelling, many cells burst (lysis).
options: Correct: hypotonic surroundings drive water in, and an animal cell has no wall to stop it bursting.
Shriveling (crenation) happens in a hypertonic solution, where water leaves the cell.
Red blood cell membranes are full of aquaporins; water crosses them quickly.
Animal cells have no cell wall; that is why they burst instead of becoming turgid.

why.correct: Side 2 has more solute, so its water potential is lower. Water moves from side 1 into side 2, and the side 2 level rises until the extra weight of the taller column balances the pull.
options: Correct: water moves toward lower water potential, the more concentrated side, raising its level.
Water moves toward the side with more solute, not less.
The membrane does not let sucrose through, so only water can move.
Water still crosses, even though sucrose cannot; that net flow of water is osmosis.

why.correct: Glucose crosses and spreads until it is equal on both sides, so it stops mattering. Sucrose cannot cross, so side 2 ends up with extra solute: its water potential is lower, and water moves into it. Only solutes that cannot cross the membrane set tonicity.
options: Correct: the crossing solute evens out, and the trapped sucrose leaves side 2 with more total solute, so water follows it there.
Equal at the start, but glucose leaves side 1 while sucrose stays put, so side 2 ends up with more solute.
Size does not make a solute attract more water; what matters is how many dissolved particles cannot cross.
Once glucose has spread evenly, side 2 still has all the sucrose on top of its glucose, so the two sides do not balance.

why.correct: Pond water is strongly hypotonic to the cell, so water floods in and the vacuole must bail it out often. Adding salt narrows the difference, less water enters, and the vacuole empties less often.
options: Correct: the closer the outside is to the cell's own solute level, the slower water enters, and the less bailing is needed.
Adding salt makes the outside less hypotonic, not more; a more hypotonic outside would make the vacuole work harder.
The contractile vacuole removes water; the data fit a simple drop in water entry without any change in its job.
If water still entered as fast and the vacuole emptied more slowly, the cell would swell and burst; the data show reduced water entry.

why.correct: Fresh water is hypotonic to the fish, so water keeps entering by osmosis and salts keep leaking out. Its kidneys get rid of the extra water as dilute urine, and gill cells take salts back in, spending ATP.
options: Correct: dump extra water, recover lost salts.
That is how a saltwater fish copes: it loses water to the sea, so it drinks and gets rid of salt.
Saving water would make its problem worse; water is already pouring in.
Blood that dilute could not keep the fish's cells working; osmoregulation keeps the blood far saltier than the surrounding water.

why.correct: Only a solution isotonic to the cells leaves their volume unchanged. Hypotonic fluids swell them and can burst them; hypertonic fluids shrink them.
options: Isotonic: water moves in and out at equal rates, so the cells keep their size.
Distilled water is strongly hypotonic and would burst red blood cells.
A hypertonic fluid would draw water out and make the cells shrivel.
Half as concentrated is hypotonic, so the cells would take in water and swell.

why.correct: Dissolved salt makes the soil water's solute potential more negative. Once soil water potential falls close to or below that of the root cells, water stops flowing in, the cells lose turgor, and the plant wilts.
options: Correct: salty soil water has a low water potential, so the gradient that draws water into roots shrinks or reverses.
Adding solute lowers water potential; it never raises it.
Salt entering root cells would lower their water potential and draw water in, which would not cause wilting.
Salt does not dissolve cellulose walls; wilting comes from water loss and the drop in turgor.

why.correct: Pure water at normal air pressure is the reference point, Ψ = 0. Any dissolved solute lowers water potential below zero.
options: Correct: with no solutes and no extra pressure, pure water in an open beaker has Ψ = 0, the highest of these.
Sucrose lowers the solute potential below zero, and an open beaker adds no pressure, so its Ψ is negative.
Turgor raises a plant cell's water potential, but at most it brings it up to 0, never above pure water's.
Salt lowers water potential even more than the same concentration of sucrose, because each unit splits into two ions.

why.correct: Osmosis depends on the number of dissolved particles. NaCl splits into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so 0.1 mol/L NaCl gives about 0.2 mol/L of particles, twice the glucose side. Side 2 has the lower water potential, so water moves into it.
options: Correct: side 2 has the higher osmolarity (about 0.2 against 0.1), so it is hypertonic and draws water.
Particle number, not particle size, sets water potential.
Same amount of substance, but not the same number of particles: NaCl doubles because it splits into two ions.
Ions attract water molecules (they are surrounded by water's partial charges); they do not repel it.

why.correct: As water enters, the contents press on the wall and the wall presses back. That pressure raises the cell's water potential until it matches the outside, and net entry stops. The cell is turgid instead of burst.
options: Correct: the wall turns swelling into pressure (turgor), and pressure raises water potential until water stops entering.
Water entry stops because pressure balances it, not because channels close.
Contractile vacuoles do this in some single-celled organisms; a plant's central vacuole stores water rather than pumping it out.
If the cell's water potential were higher, water would leave it; in a hypotonic solution water enters.

why.correct: A ratio above 1 means glucose is more concentrated inside than outside. Glucose kept entering after that point, so it was moving from low to high concentration.
options: Correct: once the ratio passes 1, each further rise means glucose moving uphill, into the more concentrated side.
A fast start then slowing happens in passive transport too; on its own it says nothing about direction relative to the gradient.
This compares two conditions; it shows ouabain matters, but not that the control moved glucose uphill.
Error bars show how much the samples varied, not which way glucose moved.

why.correct: Glucose climbs its gradient only by riding along with Na⁺ flowing down Na⁺'s gradient. Remove outside Na⁺ and that energy source is gone; glucose can still move passively, but only until the inside equals the outside (ratio 1.0).
options: Correct: without Na⁺ flowing in, nothing pays for uphill glucose movement, so the ratio stops at 1.
The cotransporter is specific for Na⁺; if choline could drive it, glucose would still pile up above a ratio of 1, which it does not.
The cotransporter does not use ATP directly; and glucose did enter, reaching a ratio of 1.0.
Na⁺ was replaced by an equal concentration of choline, so the solution's solute level did not change.

why.correct: A gradient is stored energy. When the pump stops, the Na⁺ gradient built before the drug was added still powers the cotransporter, but Na⁺ entering is no longer pumped out. As the gradient runs down, it can no longer hold glucose above the outside level.
options: Correct: the stored gradient lasts a while, then runs down without the pump to rebuild it.
Ouabain acts on the sodium-potassium pump, not the cotransporter; the delay comes from the gradient running down.
Ouabain stops the pump from using ATP; it does not stop ATP production. The cotransporter uses the Na⁺ gradient, not ATP.
If the cells were using glucose, the control would show the same fall. It keeps rising, so the fall must come from the pump being stopped.

why.correct: Simply removing Na⁺ would make the solution hypotonic to the cells, so they would swell. Then any change in glucose uptake could come from the swelling instead of the missing Na⁺. Swapping in choline, an ion the cells do not transport, changes one variable only.
options: Correct: matching total solute keeps the solution isotonic, so the only difference from the control is which ion is present.
The point of the condition is to remove the ion that drives glucose uphill, not to replace its job.
Normal solutions already contain K⁺; the swap was about keeping solute concentration constant.
Glucose is uncharged, so the solution's charge would not attract it; and swapping one positive ion for another leaves the charge unchanged.

why.correct: Inside ÷ outside = 5.0, so inside = 5.0 × 5 mM = 25 mM: five times the outside level, built by cotransport with Na⁺.
A higher pH means fewer H⁺. With the pump blocked, H⁺ stopped being pushed out, and the outside pH rose toward the inside value.
options: Correct: from 5.5 to 6.9 is a rise in pH, so the concentration of H⁺ outside fell.
The control is 5.5 and the blocker 6.9, so pH rose, not fell.
ATP was 104% of control, essentially unchanged; the pump stopped because it was blocked, not for lack of ATP.
Cytoplasm pH went from 7.5 to 7.3, a small change; the large change was outside the membrane.

why.correct: The pH scale is logarithmic: each pH unit is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration. Outside is pH 5.5 and inside pH 7.5, two units apart, so H⁺ is 10 × 10 = 100 times more concentrated outside.
