The carrier uses the energy of H⁺ flowing back in, not ATP. ATP powers only the pump, which builds that H⁺ gradient. Block the pump and the gradient collapses (pH outside rose to 6.9), so sucrose uptake falls even with plenty of ATP.
options: Correct: ATP is spent by the pump; the carrier spends the H⁺ gradient. No gradient, no uptake.
The carrier does not use ATP directly; that is what makes its transport secondary active transport.
The H⁺ leak chemical, which leaves the pump alone, cuts uptake just as much, so the gradient, not damage to the carrier, explains the drop.
The data show uptake falling; nothing suggests sucrose was taken in and lost again through the wall.

why.correct: Cotransport needs the gradient, not just the proteins. A buffer that keeps the outside at pH 7.5 removes the H⁺ gradient, so sucrose uptake drops while the carriers themselves are untouched.

variables.name: Difference in H⁺ concentration across the membrane
variables.why: With the outside held at the same pH as the cytoplasm, the H⁺ concentration difference all but disappears, however hard the pump works.

variables.name: Sucrose uptake
variables.why: The carrier depends on H⁺ flowing in down its gradient; with almost no H⁺ gradient, there is little energy to bring sucrose in.

variables.name: Number of sucrose carrier proteins in the membrane
variables.why: Changing the pH outside does not add or remove carriers within the experiment; it removes the gradient that drives them.

why.correct: Cotransport moves one substance uphill using another's downhill flow, with no ATP used by that protein. Pumps that spend ATP directly are primary active transport.
options: Sucrose moves uphill using H⁺ flowing down its gradient: cotransport.
The proton pump spends ATP directly: primary active transport.
Glucose moves uphill using Na⁺ flowing down its gradient: cotransport.
The sodium-potassium pump spends ATP directly: primary active transport.
Water moves down its own gradient through a channel: facilitated diffusion (osmosis), not active transport.

why.correct: Both move a substance uphill. The difference is the energy source: ATP spent on the protein itself (primary) or an existing gradient of another substance (secondary).
options: Correct: the source of energy separates them.
Both kinds of active transport move something against its gradient; that is what makes them active.
Moving molecules in vesicles is bulk transport. Cotransport moves single ions and molecules through proteins.
Both require membrane proteins: a pump for primary, a cotransporter for secondary.

why.correct: Opposite directions makes it an antiporter. Na⁺ enters down its gradient (built by the sodium-potassium pump), and that flow pays for pushing Ca²⁺ out against its gradient: cotransport.
options: Correct: opposite directions, and one ion's downhill flow drives the other uphill.
A symporter moves both substances the same way; here Na⁺ comes in while Ca²⁺ goes out.
No ATP is used by this protein; the energy comes from the Na⁺ gradient.
A channel lets one kind of ion run downhill; it cannot push a second ion out against its gradient.

why.correct: With fewer working pumps, Na⁺ builds up inside and the Na⁺ gradient shrinks. Less Na⁺ flows in through the exchanger, so less Ca²⁺ is pushed out, and Ca²⁺ rises inside. That extra calcium strengthens each heartbeat.
options: Correct: a smaller Na⁺ gradient is less stored energy for exporting Ca²⁺.
Extra Na⁺ inside reduces the inward Na⁺ gradient, which slows the exchanger rather than speeding it.
The exchanger does not use ATP, but it depends on the gradient the pump builds, so it is affected.
A blocked pump moves nothing, and the sodium-potassium pump does not carry calcium.

why.correct: Each glucose brings in 2 Na⁺. Pumping out 2 Na⁺ costs 2 ÷ 3 of an ATP ≈ 0.67 ATP. The cotransporter never touches ATP, but the cell still pays for every glucose, through the pump.
Sodium-glucose cotransporters move Na⁺ and glucose in together. As those solutes build up in the cells and the blood beyond, the water potential there falls, and water follows by osmosis.
options: Correct: glucose lets more Na⁺ in through cotransport, and water follows the absorbed solutes.
Pulling water into the gut would worsen dehydration; the drinks work because solutes, and then water, are absorbed.
Cells have no pumps for water; water moves by osmosis, following solutes.
Glucose and Na⁺ do not join into one molecule, and a larger polar or charged particle would cross the bilayer even less easily.

why.correct: Primary active transport fails first, because it uses ATP directly; cotransport fails soon after, because it spends the gradient the pump built; simple diffusion carries on.

variables.name: Na⁺ moved out by the sodium-potassium pump
variables.why: The pump spends ATP directly, so it slows as ATP runs out.

variables.name: Glucose built up inside the cell by sodium-glucose cotransport
variables.why: As pumping fails, Na⁺ accumulates inside and the Na⁺ gradient that drives the cotransporter runs down.

variables.name: Entry of a small nonpolar test molecule that the cell does not use, held at a fixed concentration outside
variables.why: A small nonpolar molecule crosses the bilayer by simple diffusion, which depends only on its own gradient. The cell does not use it, so stopping ATP production leaves its gradient, and its entry, unchanged.

why.correct: Uptake against a 20-fold gradient is active. Depending on outside Na⁺ but not directly on ATP is the signature of cotransport: the Na⁺ gradient lasts a while even when ATP is briefly low.
options: Correct: needs Na⁺, tolerates a short ATP dip, works uphill.
A pump that uses ATP directly would stop when ATP fell, and it would not need outside Na⁺.
Facilitated diffusion cannot build up a 20-fold excess inside; it stops when the two sides are equal.
Single amino acids are small and are carried by transport proteins; endocytosis is for large particles and fluid.

why.correct: A bacterium is far too large for any transport protein. The cell's membrane surrounds it and pinches off into a vesicle: endocytosis, a form of bulk transport that uses energy.
options: Engulfing a whole cell is phagocytosis, a kind of endocytosis.
Cotransporters move single ions and small molecules, not whole cells.
Channel proteins pass ions or water molecules, nothing close to the size of a bacterium.
A bacterium is enormous compared with the molecules that slip through the bilayer.

why.correct: Size, polarity, charge and gradient direction decide the route. Small and nonpolar means it dissolves in the bilayer; down its gradient means no energy is needed.
options: Correct: small nonpolar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂ diffuse straight through the bilayer.
A carrier is needed for molecules the bilayer blocks, such as glucose; a small nonpolar molecule does not need one.
Cotransport is for moving something uphill; this molecule is already moving downhill.
Pumps move substances against their gradient; nothing needs to be spent to let this molecule in.

why.correct: The cytoplasm links the two sides. Na⁺ entering from the gut must be pumped out somewhere to keep the inside Na⁺ low. With the pump stopped, inside Na⁺ rises and the gradient across the gut-side membrane shrinks.
options: Correct: the pump on one side keeps the whole cell's Na⁺ low, which the cotransporter on the other side depends on.
Both membranes face the same cytoplasm, so the Na⁺ level the pump sets affects the gut side too.
Na⁺ piling up inside reduces the gradient that drives the cotransporter, so uptake slows.
The cotransporter uses no ATP; its energy comes from the Na⁺ gradient.

why.correct: The lysosomal curve peaks at 100% at pH 5 and drops to 12% at pH 7, about one-eighth of its peak.
options: Correct: 100% at pH 5, 12% at pH 7.
That describes the cytosolic enzyme, which peaks at pH 7.
Activity ranges from 4% to 100%, so it changes a great deal with pH.
At pH 3 the enzyme is at 35%; it rises to its peak at pH 5 before falling.

why.correct: The lysosomal enzyme is at 12% at pH 7 and lower above it. Keeping it in an acidic compartment lets it work there, while the neutral cytosol all but switches it off if it escapes: a built-in safety feature of compartments.
options: Correct: the pH difference between the two compartments protects the cytosol.
The data show activity versus pH; nothing in them shows one enzyme breaking down the other.
Activity falls from 100% at pH 5 to 12% at pH 7, so it becomes less active in the cytosol, not more.
The cytosol (pH 7.2) is less acidic than the lysosome (pH 5), not more.

why.correct: 100% ÷ 12% ≈ 8.3. Moving the enzyme from the lysosome's pH to the cytosol's cuts its activity more than eightfold.
At pH 7 the lysosomal enzymes work at about 12% of their peak, so digestion inside the lysosome slows sharply and undigested material accumulates.
options: Correct: losing the acidic condition cripples the enzymes that need it.
The cytosolic enzyme is not inside the lysosome; raising the pH does not move it there.
The drug changes pH, not the membrane's integrity; and at pH 7 the enzymes would be weak even if they leaked.
The membrane keeps the enzymes in, but it is the acidic pH inside, which the pumps maintain, that lets them work.

why.correct: pH is the independent variable. Holding everything else constant (controlled variables) means differences in activity can be attributed to pH alone.
options: Correct: controlled variables keep other factors from explaining the pattern.
Activity still changed a great deal with pH; controlling other factors does not hold activity at its peak.
The two enzymes behaved very differently, which is the point of comparing them; they were not averaged.
Random variation still occurs, which is why each point is a mean of three trials.

why.correct: The plasma membrane is the only surface membrane, at 2%. Everything else, 100 − 2 = 98%, is internal membrane.
options: Correct: all but the plasma membrane's 2% lies inside the cell.
35% is the rough ER alone, just one of the internal membranes.
2% is the plasma membrane, the surface; the question asks about the inside.
The internal membranes add up to far more than half: rough ER and mitochondrial inner membrane alone are 67%.

why.correct: 32% ÷ 7% ≈ 4.6. The inner membrane wraps the same organelle as the outer one, yet has almost five times the area.
The inner membrane folds back and forth into cristae. Folding packs far more membrane, and so far more of the proteins that make ATP, into the same small organelle.
options: Correct: folding, not size, gives the inner membrane its extra area.
Thickness does not change area; area is measured along the membrane's surface.
There is one inner membrane, heavily folded, not several separate ones.
Liver mitochondria have intact outer membranes (7% of the cell's membrane).

why.correct: Proteins for export are made on rough ER and processed in the Golgi. Their membranes are 60% + 10% = 70% of the pancreas cell's total, much more than in the liver cell (42%).
options: Correct: a huge share of rough ER and Golgi fits a cell that secretes digestive proteins.
Smooth ER is only 1% in the pancreas cell; it is the liver cell that has much more (16%).
Mitochondrial membranes are 21% in the pancreas cell against 39% in the liver cell, a smaller share, not a larger one.
Lysosomes are grouped with other small membranes at 3%; nothing in the table singles them out.

why.correct: Check each statement against the numbers; two match.
options: Rough ER is 35% in the liver cell and 60% in the pancreas cell, the largest single entry in each.
Smooth ER is 16% in the liver cell against 1% in the pancreas cell.
The plasma membrane is 5% of the pancreas cell's membrane, one of the smallest shares.
Its mitochondrial membranes total 4% + 17% = 21%, far less than its 60% rough ER.
The shares differ a lot, for example smooth ER (16% against 1%) and rough ER (35% against 60%).

why.correct: A nucleoid is a region, not an organelle: the DNA gathers there, but no membrane separates it from the rest of the cytoplasm.
options: Correct: a DNA-rich region without a surrounding membrane.
A membrane-bound DNA compartment is a nucleus, which prokaryotes lack.
Ribosomes are scattered through the cytoplasm; the nucleoid is where the DNA is.
The cell wall is outside the plasma membrane and holds no DNA.

why.correct: Building and breaking down the same molecule in one space would undo each other in a pointless, energy-wasting cycle. Separate compartments let the cell control each process on its own.
options: Correct: separating opposing processes keeps them from cancelling each other out.
Building and breaking down use different sets of enzymes; separation is not about sharing enzymes.
The point is to control them separately, not to make them equal in rate.
The cytosol and mitochondria do not open to the outside of the cell.

why.correct: A DNA-rich nucleoid and specialized internal membranes are regions set aside for particular jobs: organization without membrane-bound organelles.
options: Correct: the nucleoid and internal membrane folds show specialized regions inside prokaryotes.
Having ribosomes is true of all cells; it does not show that parts of the cell are set aside for particular jobs.
This describes the surface membrane, not organization inside the cell.
Small size explains why prokaryotes manage without organelles; it does not show internal organization.

why.correct: Lower pH means more acidic. The lysosome (about 5) is most acidic, then the cytosol (about 7.2), then the mitochondrial matrix (about 7.8), which is slightly basic. One cell holds all three at once because membranes keep them apart.
As with the cristae of mitochondria, folding and stacking membranes multiplies the area available for membrane proteins in a small space.
options: Correct: more membrane area means room for more of the proteins that capture light.
Stacking thylakoids does not shade the stroma; its job is to add membrane area.
Thylakoids are not water channels; water crosses membranes through aquaporins.
Stacking packs in membrane without shrinking the chloroplast, and chloroplast position is a separate matter.

why.correct: Each lysosomal enzyme breaks down particular molecules. Without the one for this fat, the fat is delivered to lysosomes but not digested, so it piles up there. Inherited conditions of this kind are called lysosomal storage diseases.
options: Correct: the undigested molecule accumulates in the compartment where it should have been broken down.
Cytosolic enzymes are different enzymes; they do not take over a specific lysosomal job.
The other lysosomal enzymes still work on their own targets; only this fat's breakdown fails.
The cytosol is not acidic (about pH 7.2), and it does not digest fats this way.

why.correct: Compartments separate conditions, separate opposing processes and, through folding, add membrane area. They do not speed up movement between compartments, and the whole point is that conditions differ.
options: Separate conditions, such as the acidic lysosome inside a neutral cytosol, are a key advantage.
Separating opposing processes keeps them from undoing each other.
Cristae and thylakoids are folds that add membrane area.
Membranes are barriers; moving between organelles takes transport or vesicles, which is slower than open diffusion.
Compartments let conditions differ from place to place; they do not make them all the same.

why.correct: Spread through the whole cytosol, the molecules would be dilute. Pumped or carried into a small compartment, the same number of molecules is far more concentrated, so they meet their enzymes more often.
options: Correct: a small, enclosed space keeps reactants concentrated where they are used.
Enzymes are still needed; a membrane does not speed up the reaction itself.
Diffusion is not faster inside organelles; the gain comes from concentration, not speed.
A compartment does not change the size of the whole cell or its outer surface area.

why.correct: A double membrane with pores around the DNA is the nuclear envelope; ribosomes on membranes mean rough ER; acidic sacs are lysosomes. Membrane-bound compartments mark a eukaryote.
options: Correct: a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles identify a eukaryotic cell.
A nucleoid has no membrane around it, but this DNA is enclosed by a double membrane.
A cell wall is outside the plasma membrane; a double membrane with pores around the DNA is a nuclear envelope.
Prokaryotes do have ribosomes, so ribosomes cannot tell the two kinds apart.

why.correct: In a large cell, the outer membrane is small compared with the volume, and molecules would be dilute if spread through it. Internal membranes provide extra surface for membrane proteins and small spaces where reactants stay concentrated.
options: Correct: compartments supply surface and concentration inside the cell, offsetting some costs of large size.
Internal membranes do not change the outer membrane's area or the cell's volume, so its surface area-to-volume ratio is unchanged.
Compartments are not water stores for preventing bursting; water balance is a separate matter.
This reverses cause and effect; adding membrane does not by itself make a cell larger.

why.correct: Bacteria and mitochondria both have ribosomes near 70 S, and streptomycin cuts protein production in both, while the cytoplasm's 80 S ribosomes are almost unaffected (97%).
options: Correct: ribosome size and sensitivity to streptomycin match the bacterium, not the cytoplasm.
Chromosomes in a nucleus belong to the host cell; mitochondria have circular DNA.
That is the size of the whole plant cell; mitochondria are 1 to 10 µm, bacteria-sized.
Mitochondria form only by splitting of existing mitochondria, like bacterial fission.

why.correct: Streptomycin works by fitting bacterial ribosomes. Its strong effect on mitochondria (15%) and chloroplasts (12%), and almost none on the 80 S cytoplasmic ribosomes (97%), shows the organelles' ribosomes are built like bacterial ones, as expected if they descend from bacteria.
options: Correct: matching drug sensitivity points to matching ribosome structure, inherited from bacterial ancestors.
The data measure protein production, not death; and mitochondria cannot live on their own as bacteria do.
The cytoplasm's ribosomes are unlike bacterial ones (80 S, unaffected), which points away from a bacterial origin for the host.
The data say nothing about how easily the drug enters; the difference fits ribosome structure, which the S values confirm.

why.correct: Mitochondria make some of their own proteins on bacteria-like ribosomes. A drug that blocks bacterial ribosomes can slow that, and cells that depend most on mitochondria, such as heart and skeletal muscle and nerve cells, are hit hardest.
options: Correct: cells packed with mitochondria rely most on mitochondrial protein making.
Cells with no mitochondria have no bacteria-like ribosomes at all, so the drug has nothing in them to block.
The cytoplasm's 80 S ribosomes are barely affected (97%), so dividing cells are not the main target.
The cytoplasm of large cells still has 80 S ribosomes; size alone does not add bacteria-like ribosomes.

why.correct: Evidence for a bacterial origin is a feature the chloroplast shares with bacteria, or one that engulfing would produce. Where chloroplasts occur and what they do are facts about their job and distribution, not their origin.
options: Circular DNA matches bacteria and differs from the host's chromosomes in the nucleus.
Ribosomes near 70 S match bacterial ribosomes, not the host's 80 S ones.
Splitting of existing chloroplasts resembles binary fission; the cell cannot build them from scratch.
Two membranes fit a bacterial origin: in the engulfing model, the inner comes from the bacterium and the outer from the host membrane that wrapped around it.
This tells you which organisms have chloroplasts, which bears on when they were gained, not on whether they came from bacteria.
The green substance explains what chloroplasts do; any photosynthetic structure would need something like it, whatever its origin.

why.correct: Treated mitochondria made 15% as much protein as untreated ones, so production fell by 100 − 15 = 85%.

The host engulfed the bacterium the way a cell takes in a particle by endocytosis: its plasma membrane closed around it. In this model the inner membrane is the bacterium's own and the outer comes from the host.
options: Correct: the engulfing membrane becomes the outer layer around the bacterium.
A cell wall is not a membrane, and it does not turn into one; the model shows the host's membrane wrapping around.
The model shows a single bacterium being taken in.
The model's outer membrane forms where the host's surface wraps around the bacterium, not from the nucleus.

why.correct: The model shows step 3 (mitochondria) before step 4 (chloroplast, in one line). Every descendant of the first event has mitochondria; only descendants of the later event have chloroplasts as well.
options: Correct: the order of events explains why one organelle is nearly universal and the other limited to one group.
The model has mitochondria first; nothing in it shows animals losing chloroplasts.
The model shows two separate events, and the organelles differ in membranes, DNA and job.
Cell size does not explain the pattern; the order and branching of the events does.

why.correct: The model says mitochondria descend from bacteria, not from the host. If that is right, their DNA should resemble the DNA of living bacteria more than the host's own DNA, and it does.
options: Correct: a close DNA match to bacteria tests the model's central claim about where mitochondria came from.
